item.title: Why I’m Excited to Work with FUSION and FORESIGHT
item.description:
One of the most exciting parts of my PhD journey has been working in the FUSION research environment at the University of Galway and contributing to research connected with FORESIGHT.

FUSION stands for FUture Sustainable economy Integrated mOdelling Network. What attracts me to the group is that it does not treat sustainability as a problem that belongs to one discipline. Its work brings together life-cycle assessment, integrated assessment modelling, land-use analysis and environmental software engineering. The common thread is the use of quantitative models to ask practical questions about how economies, food systems and landscapes could change in the future.

That way of thinking fits naturally with the questions that interest me.

Agriculture and land use are full of difficult trade-offs. A national climate target can look clear on paper, but implementation happens through real production systems, farms, forests and communities. A pathway that appears technically feasible at national scale may look very different once land availability, livestock systems, economic incentives, spatial variation and alternative uses of land are considered.

This is where FORESIGHT, or Future ORiEnted ScenarIo modellinG of Holistic land use sTrategies, becomes especially interesting. The project provides agriculture and land-use modelling evidence for Ireland and continues the development of integrated AFOLU modelling tools such as GOBLIN. Its emphasis is not simply on predicting one future. It is about exploring plausible pathways, testing assumptions and understanding what different choices could mean for emissions, land use, resilience and wider sustainability objectives.

For me, that distinction matters. Forecasting asks what is likely to happen. Foresight asks a broader question: what futures are possible, what would be required to reach them, and what might we learn by working backwards from those outcomes?

My own work increasingly sits in that space. I am interested in taking national agricultural and land-use pathways and resolving them into more detailed spatial and farm-level questions. Where does adjustment occur? Which production systems are most exposed? What alternatives are actually feasible in particular places? How do economic and behavioural responses change the picture? And how can models become reusable decision-support tools rather than one-off academic exercises?

Working alongside researchers developing GOBLIN and related modelling approaches has reinforced something I increasingly value in research: the model itself is not the final product. The useful output is better evidence for a difficult decision.

That is what makes FUSION and FORESIGHT exciting to me. They create a space where environmental science, economics, modelling and software can meet around real policy problems, while keeping the analytical work transparent and open to improvement.

I expect many posts on this site will grow from that environment. Some will explain models and methods. Others will discuss new papers, data, land-use questions, agriculture, bioenergy or interesting developments in Ireland, the United States and elsewhere.

The aim is simple: use the blog as a place to think in public, connect research to current questions, and make technical work easier to understand.

item.title: From Econometrics to Scenario Thinking
item.description:
For a long time, most of my research began with data from the past.

I worked with econometric models to examine relationships, test hypotheses and understand how economic, technological and environmental variables moved together. The questions were usually backward-looking in the best sense of the term: what happened, what was associated with what, and what can the observed data tell us?

That way of thinking is still important to me. But my PhD has gradually pushed me toward a different kind of question.

Instead of asking only what happened?, I now spend much more time asking:

What could happen? What would have to change for it to happen? Where would those changes fall? And what would implementation look like for different people and places?

That shift sounds small, but it changes the entire research process.

Econometrics usually begins with observed variation. Scenario thinking often begins with a future condition, a policy target or a set of assumptions that may never have existed in the historical data. A country may set a climate-neutrality target for 2050, for example. There is no historical dataset showing how that exact transition already happened. The researcher has to construct plausible pathways, make assumptions explicit and test what follows from them.

This is where scenario modelling, foresight and backcasting become useful.

Strategic foresight is not simply forecasting. The OECD describes it as a way of exploring multiple plausible futures and preparing for the opportunities and challenges they may create. The European Commission similarly emphasises that scenarios are not predictions. They are ways of thinking systematically about how different futures might unfold.

Backcasting turns the direction around again. Instead of projecting today’s trends forward, it starts with a future objective and asks what would have to happen between that future and the present.

I find that distinction especially useful for climate, agriculture and land-use policy. A target can be clear at national level while saying very little about implementation. If livestock numbers change, where does that adjustment occur? If land is released, what can it realistically support? If a policy looks affordable in aggregate, are its costs concentrated among particular farms or regions?

Those are not questions that one method can answer on its own.

I have also learned that the divide between econometrics and scenario modelling is not as clean as it first appears. Econometric models can support forecasts and counterfactual scenarios, and historical evidence can discipline assumptions about future behaviour. In energy policy, researchers have long combined top-down economic models with more detailed sector or technology models because each sees something the other misses.

So I do not think of my research as moving away from econometrics.

It feels more like moving from a single window to a room with several windows.

Econometrics helps me ask what the observed world can teach us. Scenario modelling asks what different future worlds might require. Spatial models ask where change would occur. Microsimulation asks how apparently uniform policies can produce very different effects across heterogeneous units.

The interesting part is not choosing one of them.

It is knowing which question each method is capable of answering, and where its limits begin.

Further reading

  • OECD Strategic Foresight
  • European Commission: How do we build scenarios in a foresight exercise?
  • UK Government Futures Toolkit
  • World Bank macro-modelling and counterfactual scenario analysis
